title: Etiquette & language
body:
Spanish is universal, spoken in the fast Rioplatense accent shared with Buenos Aires — "vos" replaces "tú", and "ll"/"y" sound like the "sh" in "shore" ("yo" comes out closer to "sho"). A cheek kiss (one, right cheek) is the standard greeting between acquaintances, including a man and a woman meeting for the first time — a handshake reads as unusually formal.

Mate (a shared, bitter herbal tea sipped through a metal straw from a gourd) is a genuine daily ritual, not a tourist prop — Uruguayans carry a thermos of hot water and a mate gourd everywhere, including the beach and the bus. If offered a sip in a social setting, it's polite to accept; you drink, then pass it back to the same person (who refills and passes it on), not around a circle to your neighbor.

Restaurant tipping ("propina") is customary but not obligatory — about 10% for good service, left in cash even when the bill is paid by card. A "cubierto" or per-head cover charge on a restaurant bill pays for bread and table setting; it goes to the house, not the server, so it doesn't replace the tip. Dinner runs late by US standards — most Uruguayans eat from 21:00, and a restaurant that looks empty at 20:00 is normal, not a bad sign.
